\paragraph{Method selection.}
The M1/M2 framework guides practitioners toward the appropriate fix without exhaustive ablation. If only M2 is active ($h$ large enough to preserve task-relevant information), per-step credit methods---Turn-PPO~\cite{turnppo2025}, HCAPO~\cite{hcapo2026}, GiGPO~\cite{feng2025gigpo}---directly address sign misattribution. If only M1, increasing $h$ or full-context encoding suffices. When both co-occur (the typical default), episode-level methods address both simultaneously. Finer-grained credit methods should be applied only after establishing an episode-level baseline, as they assume correct gradient direction.

\paragraph{Extension to non-binary rewards.}
Propositions 1--2 assume binary reward ($r \in \{0, 1\}$). Our experimental setting uses a ternary scheme with a format penalty ($r \in \{-0.1, 0, 1\}$). The penalty introduces within-group reward variance even among failed episodes: a group may contain both $r = 0$ (task failure, correct format) and $r = -0.1$ (format violation) outcomes. This partial variance breaks the perfect correlation between advantage sign and episode outcome that drives the binary-case bound of $\leq$19.1\% (Proposition~2). Concretely, failed episodes with $r = 0$ can receive positive advantage when grouped with penalized episodes ($r = -0.1$), creating correct-sign updates that are absent in the binary case. The measured credit agreement of 52.07\% (Section~\ref{sec:sign_verification}) is thus consistent with theoretical expectations: substantially above the binary bound but far below the 100\% achievable with episode-level advantage. A detailed quantitative analysis appears in Appendix~\ref{app:sign_fundamental}.

30	\textit{Penalty reward effect on credit agreement.} Proposition~2 predicts 19.1\% correct-sign rate (i.e., 80.9\% incorrect) under pure binary reward. Our experiments include a $-0.1$ penalty per invalid action, making the reward non-binary. This penalty introduces variance within failed episodes: windows with valid actions receive $R_k = 0$ while windows with invalid actions receive $R_k = -0.1h$. Within a failed episode, the penalty-induced variance can occasionally produce positive $\hat{A}_k$ for windows with valid actions even when $\mu > 0$, since the normalization accounts for intra-group variance. This shifts the empirical credit agreement from the theoretical 19.1\% toward 52\%---still marginally above the 50\% random baseline ($p{=}0.025$; $+$2pp effect size) and far below the level needed for convergence. A binomial test formally rejects $H_0{:}\, P = 0.191$ ($z = 45.9$, $p < 10^{-100}$), confirming that the gap between 19.1\% (binary theory) and 52\% (penalty-reward measurement) reflects the reward structure difference, not a failure of the theoretical framework.

As $K$ increases to 16, $(1-p)^{K} \approx 0.118$, and $P(\text{correct} \mid \text{update}) \approx 14.2\%$. In the large-$K$ limit, $P(\text{correct} \mid \text{update}) \to p$, so approximately $1 - p = 87.5\%$ of all gradient updates for locally correct windows point in the wrong direction.
